proofs.proof_tex:
By \(\mathrm{lem{:}initial\mbox{-}score\mbox{-}clt}\), the following identity is exact on every retained row:
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\tau_n-\tau_n)
 =b_n^{\mathsf T}D_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}})
   +s_nE_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}}). \tag{1}
\]
By \(\mathrm{thm{:}radial\mbox{-}entrance\mbox{-}law\mbox{-}design\mbox{-}class}\),
\[
 \bigl(D_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}}),E_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}})\bigr)
 \Rightarrow(C_{k,a},\varepsilon),
 \qquad C_{k,a}\perp\varepsilon. \tag{2}
\]
The hypotheses \(b_n\to b\) and \(s_n\to s\) are deterministic.  Apply the continuous mapping theorem to the joint vector in (2), together with deterministic Slutsky convergence, in the continuous map
\((d,e,\widetilde b,\widetilde s)\mapsto\widetilde b^{\mathsf T}d+\widetilde s e\).  Equation (1) then yields
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\tau_n-\tau_n)
 \Rightarrow b^{\mathsf T}C_{k,a}+s\varepsilon. \tag{3}
\]
The independence in (3) is the independence in (2).  Throughout, \(\tau_n\) remains the fixed finite-population causal contrast from \(\mathrm{def{:}ate\mbox{-}estimator}\); the right-hand side of (3) is its design-randomization limit and is not a redefinition of that estimand.

The joint functional-limit theorem gives \(T_n/n=O_{\Pr}(1)\).  Fix \(\eta>0\).  There is \(L<\infty\) such that
\[
 \limsup_{n\to\infty}\Pr(T_n>nL)<\eta. \tag{4}
\]
Apply the actual-path arm-uniformity conclusion used in the characteristic theorem to the following finite collection of bounded deterministic arrays:
\[
 1,\quad x_{nij},\quad x_{nij}x_{ni\ell},\quad
 Y_{ni}(z),\quad x_{nij}Y_{ni}(z),\quad Y_{ni}(z)^2,
 \qquad z\in\{0,1\},\quad 1\le j,\ell\le k. \tag{5}
\]
The uniform boundedness assumption supplies a common finite envelope for (5); since the family is finite, its parameter set is compact and its Lipschitz requirement is vacuous.  On \(\{T_n\le nL\}\), the arm-uniformity conclusion, evaluated at \(m=T_n\), says that every treated- and control-arm raw empirical moment in (5) differs from its finite-population counterpart by \(o_{\Pr}(1)\).  By (4), the probability of the complementary event is at most \(\eta+o(1)\).  Letting \(\eta\downarrow0\) proves the same assertion without conditioning on the stopping event.

Centered covariances are polynomial functions of the raw moments in (5).  Hence, for \(z\in\{0,1\}\), the observed arm Gram matrix and outcome--covariate covariance satisfy
\[
 \widehat S_{xx,z,n}-S_{xx,n}=o_{\Pr}(1),
 \qquad
 \widehat c_{z,n}-S_{x,Y(z),n}=o_{\Pr}(1), \tag{6}
\]
where replacing an \(n/2\) divisor by its degrees-of-freedom correction changes the quantities by \(o(1)\).  On the retained tail, \(\lambda_{\min}(S_{xx,n})\ge c_x/2\).  Weyl's inequality applied to (6) therefore gives
\[
 \Pr\!\left\{\min_{z\in\{0,1\}}\lambda_{\min}
   (\widehat S_{xx,z,n})\ge c_x/4\right\}\longrightarrow1. \tag{7}
\]
On the event in (7), the inverse map is continuous on matrices whose least eigenvalue is at least \(c_x/4\), so
\(\widehat S_{xx,z,n}^{-1}-S_{xx,n}^{-1}=o_{\Pr}(1)\).
Thus the Moore--Penrose convention on the event complementary to (7) has no first-order effect.

The residual mean square from an intercept-and-slope fit is
\[
 \widehat S_{e_z,n}^2
 =\widehat S_{Y(z)Y(z),z,n}
  -\widehat c_{z,n}^{\mathsf T}
   \widehat S_{xx,z,n}^{-1}\widehat c_{z,n}
\]
on (7).  The raw-moment convergence, (6), and inverse continuity consequently imply
\[
 \widehat S_{e_z,n}^2-S_{e_ze_z,n}=o_{\Pr}(1),
 \qquad z\in\{0,1\}. \tag{8}
\]
Because \(\|S_{xx,n}^{-1/2}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\sqrt{2/c_x}\) on the retained tail, the definitions and (6) give
\[
 \begin{split}
 \widehat b_n-b_n
 &=S_{xx,n}^{-1/2}
 \bigl\{(\widehat c_{1,n}-S_{x,Y(1),n})
       +(\widehat c_{0,n}-S_{x,Y(0),n})\bigr\}
 \longrightarrow_{\Pr}0,\\
 \widehat u_n-u_n
 &=2(\widehat S_{e_1,n}^2-S_{e_1e_1,n})
   +2(\widehat S_{e_0,n}^2-S_{e_0e_0,n})
 \longrightarrow_{\Pr}0. \tag{9}
 \end{split}
\]
This proves all asserted stopped-design moment conclusions.  The argument uses uniformity along the actual pre-entry path and never replaces the terminal allocation by a uniform draw from the acceptable set.

Fix an arbitrary sequence in \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{PSRR}}\).  All probabilities below are with respect to assignment, because the fixed-potential-outcome assumption makes the finite population deterministic.  The second-moment-limit and covariate-nondegeneracy clauses of the class imply convergence of \(S_{xx,n}^{-1}\), the two arm slopes, and all projection-residual second moments.  Thus, along the retained even tail,
\[
 b_n\to b,\qquad s_n^2\to s^2,\qquad u_n\to u. \tag{10}
\]
Residual nondegeneracy gives \(s^2>0\).  Expanding \(h=Y(1)+Y(0)\) after projecting each potential-outcome array on \(x\), the definition of the residual envelope gives the exact finite-population identities
\[
 s_n^2=S_{e_1+e_0,e_1+e_0,n},\qquad
 u_n-s_n^2=S_{e_1-e_0,e_1-e_0,n}\ge0. \tag{11}
\]
Consequently \(0<s^2\le u\).  Notice that (11) is an upper envelope: it does not identify the unobserved residual treatment-effect variance.

We next prove that the critical value exists and is computable.  Write \(R=\|G\|\) and \(U=G/\|G\|\), assigning any value to \(U\) on the null event \(G=0\).  Spherical symmetry of the standard Gaussian gives \(R\sim\chi_k\), \(U\) uniform on the unit sphere, and \(R\perp U\).  Hence
\[
 (C_{k,a})_1=\min(R,\sqrt a)\,U_1. \tag{12}
\]
For \(v>0\), the distribution function of
\(X_{v,B}=|\sqrt v\,\varepsilon+B(C_{k,a})_1|\) is therefore
\[
 F_{v,B}(t)=\mathbb E_{R,U}\!\left[
 \Phi\!\left(\frac{t-B\min(R,\sqrt a)U_1}{\sqrt v}\right)
 -\Phi\!\left(\frac{-t-B\min(R,\sqrt a)U_1}{\sqrt v}\right)
 \right]. \tag{13}
\]
For \(k\ge2\), \(U_1\) has density
\[
 \frac{\Gamma(k/2)}{\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma((k-1)/2)}
 (1-u^2)^{(k-3)/2}\mathbf 1_{\{-1<u<1\}},
\]
whereas for \(k=1\) it is uniform on \(\{-1,1\}\).  Together with the chi density for \(R\), (13) is the claimed Gaussian--spherical integral.  At \(v=0\), it is interpreted as the corresponding indicator integral from (12).  Thus numerical quadrature, scalar bisection in \(t\), and compact one-dimensional maximization in \(v\) compute the critical value to any prescribed accuracy.

It remains to justify the maximum rather than merely a supremum.  Couple all \(X_{v,B}\) using the same pair \((\varepsilon,C_{k,a})\).  If \((v_j,B_j)\to(v,B)\), then \(X_{v_j,B_j}\to X_{v,B}\) almost surely.  For \(v>0\), Gaussian convolution yields a continuous positive density.  For \(v=0<B\), (12) yields positive mass in every nonempty interval contained in the interior of the support; when \(k=1\) there can additionally be an endpoint atom, but there is no gap immediately below that endpoint.  Therefore, if \(q=q_\alpha(v,B)\), then for each \(\delta>0\),
\[
 F_{v,B}((q-\delta)_+)<1-\alpha<F_{v,B}(q+\delta), \tag{14}
\]
with the left inequality omitted when \(q=0\).  Almost-sure coupling, bounded convergence at continuity points, and (14) imply
\[
 q_\alpha(v_j,B_j)\longrightarrow q_\alpha(v,B). \tag{15}
\]
At \((v,B)=(0,0)\), the bound
\[
 q_\alpha(v,B)\le B\sqrt a+\sqrt v\,q_\alpha(1,0)
\]
proves (15) directly.  Thus \(q_\alpha\) is continuous on \([0,\infty)^2\).
Writing \(v=ut\) with \(t\in[0,1]\), continuity on a compact set gives
\[
 q_{*,\alpha}(u,B)=\max_{t\in[0,1]}q_\alpha(ut,B), \tag{16}
\]
so the maximum exists.  The same compactness argument, applied to maximizing subsequences, proves continuity of \(q_{*,\alpha}\) in \((u,B)\).

Stopped-moment consistency and (10), (16) yield
\[
 q_{*,\alpha}(\widehat u_n,\|\widehat b_n\|)
 \longrightarrow_{\Pr}q_{*,\alpha}(u,\|b\|). \tag{17}
\]
Rotational invariance gives
\(b^{\mathsf T}C_{k,a}\overset d=\|b\|(C_{k,a})_1\).
By \(s^2\le u\) in (11) and the defining maximum,
\[
 q_{*,\alpha}(u,\|b\|)\ge q_\alpha(s^2,\|b\|). \tag{18}
\]
The ATE limit theorem and \(s>0\) show that the limiting absolute error has a continuous distribution.  Slutsky's theorem applied to (17), followed by (18), gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}\Pr(\tau_n\in I_n)
 &=\liminf_{n\to\infty}\Pr\!\left\{
 \left|\sqrt n(\widehat\tau_n-\tau_n)\right|
 \le q_{*,\alpha}(\widehat u_n,\|\widehat b_n\|)
 \right\}\\
 &\ge
 \Pr\!\left\{|s\varepsilon+\|b\|(C_{k,a})_1|
 \le q_\alpha(s^2,\|b\|)\right\}
 \ge1-\alpha. \tag{19}
 \end{split}
\]
This is the asserted sequencewise design-based coverage.

Finally, a four-unit enumeration verifies why the result is not finite-sample exact.  Take \(k=1\), \(a=1\),
\[
 x=(-3,-1,1,3),\qquad Y(0)=(0,0,0,0),\qquad
 Y(1)=(1,1,1,-3).
\]
Then \(S_{xx}=20/3\).  Of the six balanced allocations, the four with treated covariate sums \(0\) or \(\pm2\) are acceptable, whereas those with sums \(\pm4\) are not.  From either unacceptable allocation, each of its four treated--control transpositions is improving and leads to one of the four acceptable allocations.  Uniform initialization therefore gives every terminal acceptable allocation probability
\(1/6+2(1/6)(1/4)=1/4\), independently of finite \(\gamma\).
Here \(\tau=0\).  For each of the two terminal allocations selecting two treated units with equal treated potential outcomes, the intercept-plus-slope residuals in both observed arms vanish, so \(\widehat u=0\), \(\widehat b=0\), and \(I_n=\{1\}\), which misses \(0\).  Those allocations have total probability \(1/2\).  Thus, for example at \(\alpha=0.05\), finite-sample coverage is at most \(1/2\).  This exact stress test is consistent with, and delimits, the asymptotic claim in (19).

Let \(\widehat\beta_{z,n}\) be the within-arm OLS slope.  The centered-covariate condition and equal allocation give \(\bar x_{1,n}+\bar x_{0,n}=0\).  The coefficient on treatment in the fully interacted regression is the difference of the two fitted arm intercepts.  Hence, whenever the two arm Gram matrices are nonsingular,
\[
 \widehat\tau_{\mathrm{Lin},n}
 =\widehat\tau_n-\frac12(\widehat\beta_{1,n}+\widehat\beta_{0,n})^{\mathsf T}
 (\bar x_{1,n}-\bar x_{0,n}). \tag{20}
\]
The stopped-moment lemma gives
\(\widehat\beta_{z,n}-\beta_{z,n}=o_{\Pr}(1)\), and its eigenvalue argument shows that singularity has probability tending to zero.  Thus the Moore--Penrose convention agrees with (20) with probability tending to one.

Directly from the score definition and finite-population centering,
\[
 \bar x_{1,n}-\bar x_{0,n}
 =\frac2{\sqrt n}S_{xx,n}^{1/2}D_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}}),
 \qquad
 S_{xx,n}^{1/2}(\beta_{1,n}+\beta_{0,n})=b_n. \tag{21}
\]
The terminal design enforces
\(\|D_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}})\|\le\sqrt a\), so the product of the \(o_{\Pr}(1)\) slope error and the scaled covariate difference in (21) is \(o_{\Pr}(1)\).  Combining (20)--(21) with the exact ATE decomposition from the initial-score lemma gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 \sqrt n(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{Lin},n}-\tau_n)
 &=b_n^{\mathsf T}D_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}})
   +s_nE_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}})
   -b_n^{\mathsf T}D_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}})
   +o_{\Pr}(1)\\
 &=s_nE_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}})+o_{\Pr}(1). \tag{22}
 \end{split}
\]
The radial-entrance theorem gives
\(E_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}})\Rightarrow\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\), and \(s_n\to s>0\).  Slutsky's theorem applied to (22) proves
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{Lin},n}-\tau_n)
 \Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,s^2). \tag{23}
\]

Let \(z_{1-\alpha/2}\) be the standard-normal two-sided critical value.  The residual-Neyman interval has half-width
\(z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat u_n/n}\).
Stopped-moment consistency gives \(\widehat u_n\to_{\Pr}u\), while the variance-envelope identity gives \(u\ge s^2\).  Equations (22)--(23) and continuity of the Gaussian distribution imply
\[
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}
 \Pr\!\left\{
 \left|\sqrt n(\widehat\tau_{\mathrm{Lin},n}-\tau_n)\right|
 \le z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\widehat u_n}
 \right\}\ge1-\alpha. \tag{24}
\]
If \(u_n-s_n^2\to0\), then \(u=s^2\); the standardized limiting statistic in (24) is exactly standard normal, so the limiting coverage is exactly \(1-\alpha\).

If \(b=0\), the ATE limit theorem reduces to
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\tau_n-\tau_n)\Rightarrow s\varepsilon
 \sim\mathcal N(0,s^2). \tag{25}
\]
When \(B_0=0\), the clipped-Gaussian summand in the critical-value definition vanishes.  Hence, for every \(v\ge0\),
\[
 q_\alpha(v,0)=\sqrt v\,c_\alpha,\qquad
 c_\alpha=\inf\{t\ge0:\Pr(|\varepsilon|\le t)\ge1-\alpha\}, \tag{26}
\]
where the equality at \(v=0\) follows because both sides are zero.  The right-hand side is nondecreasing in \(v\).  Therefore
\[
 q_{*,\alpha}(u,0)
 =\max_{0\le v\le u}q_\alpha(v,0)
 =\sqrt u\,c_\alpha. \tag{27}
\]
Substituting (27) into the variance-envelope interval gives the usual conservative Neyman Gaussian half-width \(c_\alpha\sqrt{u/n}\), with \(u\) replaced in the observable interval by its stopped-design consistent estimator \(\widehat u_n\).  Thus the reduction follows from the stopped PSRR limit; no complete-randomization or uniform-acceptance law is assumed.

We prove the covariate and joint clauses separately.

For a sequence in \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{PSRR}}^x\), use the smooth extension furnished by
\(\mathrm{lem{:}covariate\mbox{-}path\mbox{-}characteristics\mbox{-}and\mbox{-}clock}\), and let
\(X_n(t)=D_n(W^x_{n,\lfloor nt\rfloor})\) denote its proposal-clock interpolation before absorption.  The extension agrees with original PSRR through \(T_n^x\).  Its limiting drift and covariance are
\[
 \beta_\phi(d)=-4d-8\gamma\phi'(\|d\|^2)d,
 \qquad c_\phi=8I_k. \tag{28}
\]
The clock conversion in that lemma already expresses (28) on the original treated--control proposal scale.

We first prove compact containment.  Stop at the first exit \(\sigma_{n,R}\) from the radius-\(R\) ball.  Sum the compactly stopped second-moment drift inequality in the characteristic lemma through
\(\lfloor nL\rfloor\wedge\sigma_{n,R}\).  The complete-randomization covariance identity gives
\(\mathbb E\|X_n(0)\|^2=k\), and the maximal score bound makes the exit overshoot \(O(n^{-1/2})\).  Markov's inequality therefore gives
\[
 \Pr\!\left\{\sup_{t\le L}\|X_n(t)\|>R\right\}
 \le\frac{k+CL+o(1)}{(R-Cn^{-1/2})^2}. \tag{29}
\]
The right-hand side is uniformly small after \(R\to\infty\).

On a fixed ball, the predictable drift rate and quadratic-variation rate are bounded, and every jump is \(O(n^{-1/2})\).  If \(\sigma_n\le L\) is a stopping time and \(\delta_n\downarrow0\), the predictable finite-variation increment over
\([\sigma_n,\sigma_n+\delta_n]\) is \(O(\delta_n+n^{-1})\), while conditional Chebyshev applied to the martingale increment yields
\[
 \Pr\{\|M_n(\sigma_n+\delta_n)-M_n(\sigma_n)\|>\eta\}
 \le C\eta^{-2}(\delta_n+n^{-1}). \tag{30}
\]
Equations (29)--(30) give tightness in \(D([0,L],\mathbb R^k)\); the vanishing maximal jump implies that every subsequential limit is continuous.

For \(f\in C_c^3(\mathbb R^k)\), Taylor's theorem and the \(O(n^{-1/2})\) jump bound give, before compact exit,
\[
 \begin{split}
 \mathbb E\{f(X_{n,(m+1)/n})-f(X_{n,m/n})\mid\mathcal F^x_{n,m}\}
 &=\nabla f(X_{n,m/n})^{\mathsf T}
   \mathbb E(\Delta D^x_{n,m}\mid\mathcal F^x_{n,m})\\
 &\quad+\frac12\nabla^2f(X_{n,m/n}):
 \mathbb E(\Delta D^x_{n,m}\Delta D^{x\mathsf T}_{n,m}
 \mid\mathcal F^x_{n,m})+O(n^{-3/2}). \tag{31}
 \end{split}
\]
The trajectory-uniform characteristic bounds make the sum through \(nL\) of the difference between (31) and
\(n^{-1}\mathcal L_\phi f(X_{n,m/n})\) converge to zero in probability, where
\[
 \mathcal L_\phi f(d)
 =\beta_\phi(d)^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(d)
  +4\operatorname{tr}\{\nabla^2f(d)\}. \tag{32}
\]
Compact stopping makes the errors bounded, so truncation upgrades this convergence to \(L^1\).  Passing the conditional martingale identity to any subsequential limit shows that, for \(0\le s<t\) and every bounded continuous path functional \(Q\) measurable through time \(s\),
\[
 \mathbb E\!\left[
 Q\left\{f(X_t)-f(X_s)-\int_s^t\mathcal L_\phi f(X_u)\,du\right\}
 \right]=0. \tag{33}
\]
Thus each limit solves the martingale problem for (32).

Because \(\phi\) is constant near zero, smooth on the transition annulus, and equal to the logarithm away from zero, the map
\(d\mapsto\phi'(\|d\|^2)d\) is globally Lipschitz.  Picard iteration therefore constructs a strong solution of the stochastic differential equation with coefficients (28).  If two solutions use the same Brownian motion, the Lipschitz bound, the elementary inequality
\(\sup_{u\le t}\|\int_0^u g_v\,dv\|^2\le t\int_0^t\|g_v\|^2\,dv\), and Gronwall's inequality give
\[
 \mathbb E\sup_{u\le t}\|X_u-X'_u\|^2
 \le C\int_0^t\mathbb E\sup_{v\le u}\|X_v-X'_v\|^2\,du=0. \tag{34}
\]
Hence the martingale problem in (33) has a unique law.  The initial-score CLT identifies \(X_0=G\), so tightness and uniqueness identify convergence of the whole extended process.

Before first entry, \(\phi'(\|D_t\|^2)=1/\|D_t\|^2\).  Applying Ito's formula to \(R_t=\|D_t\|^2\) gives
\[
 dR_t=8(k-2\gamma-R_t)\,dt+\sqrt{32R_t}\,d\beta_t,
 \qquad R_t>a, \tag{35}
\]
with generator
\[
 \mathcal L_Rg(r)=16r g''(r)+8(k-2\gamma-r)g'(r). \tag{36}
\]
A scale derivative is
\(s'(r)=e^{r/2}r^{\gamma-k/2}\), since direct differentiation gives \(\mathcal L_Rs=0\).  Let
\(H_a=\inf\{t:R_t\le a\}\) and \(H_M=\inf\{t:R_t\ge M\}\).
Optional stopping of the bounded martingale
\(s(R_{t\wedge H_a\wedge H_M})\) gives, for \(a<r<M\),
\[
 \Pr_r(H_M<H_a)=\frac{s(r)-s(a)}{s(M)-s(a)}. \tag{37}
\]
The denominator tends to infinity with \(M\).  On every compact interval \([a,M]\), the diffusion coefficient in (35) is bounded away from zero.  Solving the linear boundary-value equation
\(\mathcal L_Rg=-1\), \(g(a)=g(M)=0\), gives a bounded nonnegative \(C^2\) solution; Ito's formula then shows that the exit time from \((a,M)\) has finite expectation.  Letting \(M\to\infty\) in (37) proves \(H_a<\infty\) almost surely from every \(r>a\).  For \(r\le a\), \(H=0\).

The Gaussian initialization has no mass on \(R_0=a\).  At a hit from outside, the martingale coefficient in (35) equals \(\sqrt{32a}>0\).  In a sufficiently small neighborhood of \(a\), its quadratic variation is strictly increasing and its drift is bounded.  The associated Brownian time change and the reflection principle show that the path cannot remain on the exterior side for any positive interval after hitting \(a\).  Hence it crosses immediately into \((0,a)\) almost surely.  Initial strict-interior paths have hitting time zero stably, while exterior paths have a finite boundary hit followed immediately by a strict-interior crossing.  Therefore the closed-ball first-hit functional is continuous at almost every limiting path.  Together with the vanishing discrete terminal jump from the characteristic lemma, the continuous mapping theorem on \([0,L]\), followed by \(L\to\infty\), yields
\[
 (\bar D_n^x,T_n^x/n)\Rightarrow(D_{\cdot\wedge H},H). \tag{38}
\]

Let \(A_n^x\) be the accepted-switch count, and let \(R_n(L)\) count rejections through
\(\lfloor nL\rfloor\wedge T_n^x\).  The covariate characteristic-and-clock lemma gives
\(R_n(L)=O_{\Pr}(\sqrt n)\).  For every \(\eta>0\),
\[
 \Pr\{(T_n^x-A_n^x)/n>\eta\}
 \le\Pr\{T_n^x>nL\}+\Pr\{R_n(L)>\eta n\}. \tag{39}
\]
For fixed \(L\), the second term tends to zero; tightness of \(T_n^x/n\) from (38) makes the first arbitrarily small by increasing \(L\).  This proves the accepted-switch/proposal-clock equivalence.

We now derive the transform of the proposal-time entrance law.  Put
\[
 A=\lambda/8>0,\qquad b=k/2-\gamma,\qquad
 U(A,b,x)=\frac1{\Gamma(A)}
 \int_0^\infty e^{-xt}t^{A-1}(1+t)^{b-A-1}\,dt. \tag{40}
\]
The integral is finite and positive.  Differentiation under the integral is justified by integrability at zero and the exponential tail.  One integration by parts then gives Kummer's equation
\[
 xU_{xx}+(b-x)U_x-AU=0. \tag{41}
\]
Define \(u_\lambda(r)=U(A,b,r/2)/U(A,b,a/2)\).  Substitution of (41) into (36) gives
\[
 \mathcal L_Ru_\lambda=\lambda u_\lambda,\qquad u_\lambda(a)=1. \tag{42}
\]
Changing variables \(z=xt\) in (40), followed by dominated convergence, gives
\(U(A,b,x)\sim x^{-A}\) as \(x\to\infty\), and hence \(u_\lambda(r)\to0\).
Ito's formula makes
\[
 e^{-\lambda(t\wedge H_a\wedge H_M)}
 u_\lambda(R_{t\wedge H_a\wedge H_M})
\]
a bounded martingale.  Let first \(t\to\infty\) and then \(M\to\infty\).  Equation (37), the almost-sure finiteness of \(H_a\), and \(u_\lambda(M)\to0\) yield
\[
 \mathbb E_r(e^{-\lambda H})=
 \begin{cases}
 1,&r\le a,\\[1mm]
 \displaystyle
 \frac{U(\lambda/8,k/2-\gamma,r/2)}
 {U(\lambda/8,k/2-\gamma,a/2)},&r>a.
 \end{cases} \tag{43}
\]
Integrating (43) against the \(\chi_k^2\) density and separating the event \(R_0\le a\) gives
\[
 \mathbb E(e^{-\lambda H})
 =F_{\chi_k^2}(a)+
 \frac{\displaystyle\int_a^\infty
 U(\lambda/8,k/2-\gamma,r/2)r^{k/2-1}e^{-r/2}\,dr}
 {\displaystyle2^{k/2}\Gamma(k/2)
 U(\lambda/8,k/2-\gamma,a/2)}. \tag{44}
\]
At \(\lambda=0\), the transform is one by definition.

The tuning dependence is strict.  Let \(\gamma_2>\gamma_1\) and let \(u_j\) be (43) for \(\gamma_j\).  The integral representation shows \(u'_2(r)<0\).  Therefore
\[
 (\mathcal L_{R,\gamma_1}-\lambda)u_2
 =16(\gamma_2-\gamma_1)u'_2<0. \tag{45}
\]
The one-dimensional maximum principle on \([a,M]\), followed by \(M\to\infty\), uses
\(u_2-u_1=0\) at \(a\) and \(u_2-u_1\to0\) at infinity to give
\(u_2(r)>u_1(r)\) for every \(r>a\).  Hence (43), and also the unconditional transform (44), is strictly increasing in finite \(\gamma\).

Finally, take a sequence in \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{PSRR}}\).  The initial-score lemma gives
\[
 Z_n(W_{n,0})\Rightarrow\mathcal N_{k+1}(0,I_{k+1}). \tag{46}
\]
The actual-filtration characteristic theorem gives, on the outcome tail, limiting drift and covariance
\[
 \beta_\phi(d,e)=
 \bigl(-4d-8\gamma\phi'(\|d\|^2)d,-4e\bigr),
 \qquad c_\phi=8I_{k+1}, \tag{47}
\]
with vanishing conditional Lindeberg terms and the same discrete terminal-crossing control.  The compact-containment, tightness, Taylor expansion, and martingale-problem arguments in (29)--(34), now in dimension \(k+1\), identify the unique solution
\[
 \begin{split}
 dD_t&=\{-4D_t-8\gamma\phi'(\|D_t\|^2)D_t\}\,dt+\sqrt8\,dB_t,\\
 dE_t&=-4E_t\,dt+\sqrt8\,dB'_t.
 \end{split} \tag{48}
\]
The identity covariance in (47) and the independent Gaussian coordinates in (46) permit \(B,B'\) and \(G,\varepsilon\) to be taken mutually independent.  This independence is derived from the limiting martingale problem, not assumed of the finite-population scores.  Since the hitting argument and stopping functional depend only on \(D\), the same transfer that proved (38) gives
\[
 (\bar Z_n,T_n/n)\Rightarrow
 \left(\bigl((D_{t\wedge H}^{\mathsf T},E_{t\wedge H})^{\mathsf T}\bigr)_{t\ge0},H\right). \tag{49}
\]
Before \(H\), (48) is exactly the system in
\(\mathrm{def{:}limit\mbox{-}system}\); absorption at \(H\) proves the joint clause and its uniqueness.  No projected Markov property was used.

The two-class functional theorem gives convergence of the stopped covariate path and the finite hitting time.  On \(\{\|G\|^2<a\}\), one has \(H=0\) and \(D_H=G\).  There is no boundary ambiguity because the chi-square law is continuous and hence
\(\Pr(\|G\|^2=a)=0\).  On \(\{\|G\|^2>a\}\), continuity of \(D\) gives
\[
 \|D_H\|=\sqrt a. \tag{50}
\]
For every orthogonal \(k\times k\) matrix \(Q\), the drift and diffusion in the exterior equation obey
\[
 \beta(Qd)=Q\beta(d),\qquad QI_kQ^{\mathsf T}=I_k. \tag{51}
\]
The initial Gaussian law and the stopping ball are also invariant under \(Q\).  Uniqueness in law of the stopped diffusion therefore gives
\[
 QD_H\overset d=D_H. \tag{52}
\]
The only rotation-invariant probability measure on the sphere of radius \(\sqrt a\) is normalized surface measure.  Thus the exterior branch in (50) is uniform in direction and has mass
\(\Pr(\|G\|^2>a)\).  The interior branch retains the original Gaussian law.  Since a spherical Gaussian has uniform direction independent of its radius, these two branches together are precisely
\[
 D_H\overset d=
 G\min\{1,\sqrt a/\|G\|\}=C_{k,a}. \tag{53}
\]
Convergence in the functional theorem, evaluated at the absorbed endpoint, proves the outcome-free assertion
\[
 D_n(W^x_{n,T_n^x})\Rightarrow C_{k,a}. \tag{54}
\]
No coefficient in the argument leading to (53) depends on \(\gamma\) except the radial search speed, so every fixed finite tuning has this same endpoint law.

On the outcome-inference subclass, the residual coordinate has the explicit representation
\[
 E_t=e^{-4t}\varepsilon+\sqrt8\int_0^t e^{-4(t-u)}\,dB'_u. \tag{55}
\]
Its variance at every deterministic \(t\) is
\[
 e^{-8t}+8\int_0^t e^{-8(t-u)}\,du=1, \tag{56}
\]
so \(E\) is stationary standard Gaussian.  The entire residual process is independent of the covariate process, and \(H\) is measurable with respect to the latter.  Consequently, for bounded measurable \(f\) and every bounded covariate-path functional \(Q\),
\[
 \mathbb E\{f(E_H)Q(D)\}
 =\mathbb E\{f(\varepsilon)\}\mathbb E\{Q(D)\}. \tag{57}
\]
Thus \(E_H\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\) and \(E_H\perp D_H\).  The joint functional convergence now yields
\[
 \bigl(D_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}}),E_n(W_{n,\mathrm{stop}})\bigr)
 \Rightarrow(C_{k,a},\varepsilon),
 \qquad C_{k,a}\perp\varepsilon. \tag{58}
\]
This independence follows from the block-diagonal limiting characteristics and stationarity, not from an outcome--residual independence assumption on the finite arrays.

Finally, (53) gives
\[
 \|C_{k,a}\|^2=\min\{\|G\|^2,a\}
 =\min\{\chi_k^2,a\}, \tag{59}
\]
and therefore
\[
 \Pr\{\|C_{k,a}\|^2=a\}
 =1-F_{\chi_k^2}(a)>0, \tag{60}
\]
because \(k\ge1\) and \(0<a<\infty\).  The transform proved in the two-class theorem shows that \(\gamma\) nevertheless changes the proposal-time search law.  The distinction from \(L_{k,a}\) is certified in the following proposition.

The clipped-Gaussian definition and continuity of the chi-square distribution give
\[
 \Pr\{\|C_{k,a}\|^2=a\}
 =\Pr\{\|G\|^2\ge a\}
 =1-F_{\chi_k^2}(a)>0. \tag{61}
\]
By contrast,
\[
 L_{k,a}\overset d=G\mid\{\|G\|^2\le a\}.
\]
Its conditional squared radius is the continuous chi-square law restricted to \([0,a]\), so
\[
 \Pr\{\|L_{k,a}\|^2=a\}=0. \tag{62}
\]
The measurable boundary sphere \(\{d:\|d\|^2=a\}\) separates the two probability measures, proving that the laws differ.

Every design in \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{PSRR}}^x\) has equal arms, uniform balanced initialization, treated--control transposition proposals, the original Metropolis acceptance rule with fixed finite tuning, and immediate stopping at the first entry into \(M_n\le a\).  These are precisely the operations in the original PSRR definition.  Boundedness, fixed dimension, second-moment convergence, and covariance nondegeneracy only restrict the deterministic covariate arrays on which that algorithm is run.  Hence \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{PSRR}}^x\) is a subclass of the broader published algorithmic domain.  Were the original algorithm's terminal output uniformly distributed on the acceptable set throughout that broader domain, its asymptotic covariate law would be \(L_{k,a}\) on every sequence in this subclass, contradicting (61)--(62).  This subclass witness refutes the universal uniform representation; it does not enlarge the positive functional-limit result beyond \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{PSRR}}^x\).
